title: Colourings with no monochromatic Pythagorean quadruple
statement: A Pythagorean quadruple is a solution of x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = w^2 in positive integers (the edges and the space diagonal of a box with integer sides; the smallest is 1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2 = 3^2, and x, y, z may repeat). Colour the integers 1, 2, ..., n with K colours. What is the largest n for which some colouring has no monochromatic quadruple, i.e. no solution with x, y, z and w all of the same colour? For K = 2 the answer is 104 (ours, exact: every 2-colouring of 1..105 has one). The headline cell is K = 3: we have a colouring of 1..473; find a 3-colouring of 1..474 or more, or prove that none exists. We do not know whether the answer for K = 3 is finite.
submission: Text file: the colours of 1, 2, ..., n as digits 0, 1, 2, in order (line breaks and lines starting with # are ignored).
score: n, the length of the colouring (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 10 November 2026: a 3-colouring of 1..473 with no monochromatic quadruple, found by an incremental SAT search (CaDiCaL through python-sat; tools/colour_sat.py)

context: Erdos and Graham asked whether every finite colouring of the positive integers has a monochromatic Pythagorean triple; for two colours Heule, Kullmann and Marek (2016) found the threshold 7825 with a 200-terabyte proof, and the question for more colours is open. Frantzikinakis, Klurman and Moreira proved that every finite colouring has a monochromatic Pythagorean pair (x and y with x^2 + y^2 or x^2 - y^2 a square), and Chow, Lindqvist and Prendiville settled diagonal quadratic equations in five or more variables (so x1^2 + x2^2 + x3^2 + x4^2 = x5^2 is partition regular). Pythagorean quadruples, with four variables, fall between the two: our exact value for two colours (104) shows that two colours do not suffice, but whether every 3-colouring of a long enough interval contains a monochromatic quadruple is open, and the threshold, if finite, is unknown.
references: M. J. H. Heule, O. Kullmann, V. W. Marek, Solving and verifying the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem via cube-and-conquer, SAT 2016, LNCS 9710 (2016) 228-245
N. Frantzikinakis, O. Klurman, J. Moreira, Partition regularity of Pythagorean pairs, arXiv:2309.10636
S. Chow, S. Lindqvist, S. Prendiville, Rado's criterion over squares and higher powers, J. Eur. Math. Soc. (2021)

novelty.verdict: new. Partition regularity is known for five or more squares (Chow, Lindqvist and Prendiville) and studied for Pythagorean triples and pairs; no colouring threshold, finite or infinite, was found for Pythagorean quadruples (arXiv, Crossref and web searches).
closest: The Boolean Pythagorean triples problem (Heule, Kullmann and Marek 2016): the same question for x^2 + y^2 = z^2, threshold 7825 for two colours.
Monochromatic almost-Pythagorean quadruples x^2 + y^2 w^2 = z^2 in multiplicatively dense sets (arXiv:2610.04078): a different equation and a density question.
novelty.benchmark: no colouring family for Diophantine equations other than our eisenstein-triples

baseline.text: 473 for K = 3, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 10 November 2026: the colouring in `refs/quad-pyth.txt` (incremental SAT search, tools/colour_sat.py). K = 2: exactly 104 (the SAT solver finds 1..104 colourable and proves 1..105 not; CaDiCaL, Glucose and MiniSat agree, tools/colour_exact.py).

cells.title: Colourings with {K} colours and no monochromatic Pythagorean quadruple
cells.statement: Find the largest n such that 1..n can be coloured with {K} colours without a monochromatic solution of x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = w^2.
cells.submission: Text file: the colours of 1..n as digits 0..{K}-1.
cells.exact_how: an incremental SAT search (CaDiCaL 1.9.5 through python-sat; tools/colour_sat.py) colours 1..n and proves 1..n+1 impossible; three solvers (CaDiCaL, Glucose, MiniSat) agree on the formula built from the checker's list of quadruples (tools/colour_exact.py)
cells.how: the longest colouring an incremental SAT search found in 300 seconds (tools/colour_sat.py)
